clinicalPearls: A solitary (or few) cutaneous accumulation of mast cells, usually appearing in infancy
Presents as a single red-brown or yellowish plaque or nodule, sometimes with a peau d'orange surface
Stroking produces urtication and can cause blistering in infants (a strong Darier sign)
Vigorous rubbing may provoke flushing from localised mediator release
It is benign and typically regresses spontaneously during childhood
Management is conservative with reassurance and trigger avoidance; systemic disease is rare with a solitary lesion
reference.pathophysiology: A solitary mastocytoma is a localised benign collection of mast cells within the skin, part of the cutaneous mastocytosis spectrum. Mechanical stimulation degranulates the concentrated mast cells, releasing histamine and other mediators to produce a brisk weal-and-flare and, in infants, blistering. Because the mast cell burden is limited to a small area, systemic mediator effects are uncommon, and the lesion generally involutes as the child grows.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis with a positive Darier sign
Skin biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain
Baseline tryptase if multiple lesions or systemic features
Reassurance and monitoring for spontaneous regression
redFlags: Multiple lesions or systemic symptoms suggesting broader mastocytosis
Marked flushing or hypotension on stimulation
Atypical features suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Persistence or growth into later childhood
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent, with most solitary mastocytomas regressing spontaneously during childhood and rarely causing systemic problems.
pitfalls: Provoking blistering or flushing by vigorously rubbing the lesion
Confusing it with a melanocytic or xanthogranulomatous lesion
Assuming systemic disease from a single lesion
Unnecessary excision of a self-limiting lesion
management: Conservative management with reassurance, since most solitary mastocytomas involute spontaneously during childhood
Advise avoidance of mast-cell degranulating triggers such as friction, temperature extremes and drugs like NSAIDs and opioids
Oral H1-antihistamines to control pruritus, flushing and urtication from local mediator release
Topical corticosteroids for symptomatic or blistering lesions
Reserve surgical excision for persistent, troublesome or diagnostically uncertain lesions
Monitor for spontaneous regression and review if additional lesions or systemic mediator symptoms emerge
